podcast.title: Hip-Pocket Records Releases (1966)
podcast.body: In 1966, Mercury Records participated in the Hip-Pocket Records initiative with Filco and Ford, releasing singles on the bendable plastic Flexi Disc format. These releases, featuring artists like Tommy James and Neil Diamond, were sold for $0.69 through Ford dealerships and Woolworth stores. `"They got Atlantic, Mercury, and Roulette records to release singles this way, selling them for $0.69 at four dealerships and through Woolworth stores."`

podcast.title: Conditional Signing of The Platters
podcast.body: Mercury Records signed The Platters only because Book Ram, who managed The Penguins, made it a condition for The Penguins' signing. This strategic move brought The Platters to a major label. "Ram agreed to the deal, but only on the condition that Mercury signed the platters as well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Contractual Obligation Album
podcast.body: Graham Parker, believing the label was "botching his career," recorded *The Parkerilla*, a "quicky live album," to fulfill his contract with Mercury Records, as an act of defiance and contempt. "Parker came to believe Mercury was botching his career and so in 1978 he and his band The Rumor recorded a quicky live album The Parker Rilla to fulfill his contract with the label."

podcast.title: David Bowie's Introduction to Norm O'Dam
podcast.body: In 1970, upon signing with Mercury Records, David Bowie received a collection of 7-inch singles as a welcome gift, which included Norm O'Dam's "Paralyzed." This introduction sparked Bowie's obsession with the record and artist, ultimately inspiring his "Stardust" persona. "When Bowie signed to Mercury in 1970, he was given a stack of seven-inch singles as kind of a welcome to the label gift."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distribution for The Valtones
podcast.body: Mercury Records picked up the distribution for The Valtones' record, which was popular enough to bring a "small profit" to Satellite Records. "It was popular enough that the record got picked up for distribution by Mercury, and actually brought satellite a small profit."

podcast.title: Eager to Sign The Penguins
podcast.body: Mercury Records was keen to sign The Penguins following the massive success of their hit song "Earth Angel." "Mercury records were eager to sign them."

podcast.title: Early Recording Home for Quincy Jones
podcast.body: After moving to Paris in 1957 to study music theory and work for Mercury Records' French subsidiary, Quincy Jones released his first album, *This Is How I Feel About Jazz*, under his own name on the label that same year. "In 1957, Jones moved to Paris to study music theory and work for the French subsidiary of Mercury Records, and he released his first album under his own name that year."

podcast.title: Fred Foster's Brief Tenure
podcast.body: Fred Foster spent only a brief time at Mercury Records. He left because he was keen on exploring the rockabilly market, while his superiors within the company held opposing views. "From there he moved to Mercury Records, but he only spent a brief time there. He was in favour of moving into the rockabilly market, while his superiors in the company weren't."

podcast.title: Hugo and Luigi's Early Production Career
podcast.body: Mercury Records hired Hugo and Luigi, where they transitioned from making children's records to producing pop music. It was at Mercury that they produced the controversial cover versions by Georgia Gibbs of "black records," which were deemed "ethically and musically appalling." "before being hired by Mercury Records, where they would produce among other things. The cover versions by Georgia Gibbs of Black Records that we've talked about previously, and which were both ethically and musically appalling."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Label Stance on Political Music
podcast.body: The president of Mercury Records advised Roy Hammond that releasing political songs, such as "Open Letter to the President" and "I Wasn't There But I Can Feel the Pain" from his "Sex and Soul" album, was "holding himself back." This pressure led Hammond to form his own record label to maintain artistic control over his politically conscious music. "the president of Mercury told him that they did not want political songs And that Roy was holding himself back by recording them"

podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Federal Records
podcast.body: Mercury Records, along with Book Ram, took Federal Records to court over Federal's decision to rush-release an earlier, inferior recording of "Only You" to cash in on The Platters' success with Mercury. "Federal rush released the awful original recording to Cachean and Ram and Mercury took them to court."

podcast.title: Major Label Signing of Mother Love Bone
podcast.body: Mercury Records was the major label that signed Mother Love Bone, signaling early industry interest in bands emerging from the Pacific Northwest grunge scene. "Mother Love Bone nailed a deal with Mercury records..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Norm O'Dam's Single Release
podcast.body: Mercury Records released Norm O'Dam's single "Paralyzed" in 1968. This unusual track, whose meaning was unclear to many at the time, later gained significant historical importance when it profoundly influenced David Bowie. "He did, however, manage to release a single for Mercury Records in 1968 called Paralyzed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overdubbed Tony Williams Vocals
podcast.body: After Tony Williams left The Platters, Mercury Records, convinced of his importance to the group's sound, would often overdub his lead vocals onto completed recordings made by the new Platters lineup for a period of one to two years. "Mercury would take completed recordings by the new platters lineup and overdub new lead vocals from Williams."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Poor Promotion of Graham Parker
podcast.body: Mercury Records, Graham Parker's US label, was described as "befuddled at how to promote him," which resulted in his singles failing to reach the Hot 100 and his LPs languishing at the lower ranks of the album charts. "Parker's US label Mercury Records was befuddled at how to promote him."

podcast.title: Quincy Jones's Executive Role
podcast.body: In 1961, Mercury Records, impressed with Quincy Jones's work for their French subsidiary, promoted him to the title of Vice President at Mercury U.S., a historic move making him the first black upper-level executive at a major U.S. recording company. "Mercury Records, impressed with his work for their French subsidiary, promoted Quincy to the title of Vice President at Mercury U.S., making him the first black upper-level executive at a major U.S. recording company."

podcast.title: Space Oddity Release & US Tour
podcast.body: David Bowie signed with Mercury Records, which rushed the release of the "Space Oddity" single in 1969 to capitalize on the Apollo 11 moon landing. In 1971, Mercury also sent Bowie on a US tour in an attempt to break him in America, where he charmed the press and gathered new ideas from artists like Lou Reed and Iggy Pop. "After Bowie signed to Major Label Mercury Records, they rushed release the single to capitalize on that summer's excitement over the Apollo 11 moon landing..."

podcast.body: Mercury Records was the subject of Graham Parker's "thinly veiled screed" titled "Mercury Poisoning," which was released as a final "kiss off" to the label. "As a final kiss off to the label, Parker recorded the single Mercury Poisoning, a thinly veiled screed."
